items.q: DEXA is used to assess:
items.exp: DEXA: to assess bone mass. (Book p813)

items.q: For low bone mass, the drug named is:
items.exp: Low bone mass: bisphosphonates (correct bone quantity). (Book p813)

items.q: Calcium and vitamin D supplements in CKD patients should be given with caution.
items.exp: Calcium and vit D supplements in CKD patients to be given with caution. (Book p813)

items.q: Calciphylaxis is also called:
items.exp: Calcific uremic arteriolopathy / calciphylaxis. (Book p813)

items.q: The vasculopathy of calciphylaxis affects the arterioles of the:
items.exp: Arterioles of subcutaneous and dermal plexus undergo medial calcification. (Book p813)

items.q: Calciphylaxis is precipitated by:
items.exp: Precipitated by vit-K antagonist. (Book p813)

items.q: Vitamin K in this context regenerates:
items.exp: Vit-K regeneration → matrix Gla protein. (Book p813)

items.q: In calciphylaxis, peripheral pulses are lost.
items.exp: Clinical features: pulse preserved. (Book p813)

items.q: The classic patient with calciphylaxis is:
items.exp: Female obese. (Book p813)

items.q: The skin lesion of calciphylaxis is:
opts: Ischemic necrosis of dermis / subcutaneous fat
Pitting edema of the dependent areas
Painful vesicles on an erythematous base
items.exp: Ischemic necrosis of dermic / subcutaneous fat. (Book p813)

items.q: The violaceous painful plaque of calciphylaxis evolves as:
items.exp: Violaceous painful plaque → nodule → ulcer; site: buttock or trunk. (Book p813)

items.q: The typical site of the calciphylaxis ulcer is:
items.exp: Buttock or trunk. (Book p813)

items.q: A livedo reticularis-like lesion is the commonest presentation of calciphylaxis.
opts: False — it is listed as rare
False — it is not listed at all
items.exp: Livedo reticularis like lesion (rare). (Book p813)

items.q: The diagnosis of calciphylaxis is:
items.exp: Management: clinical diagnosis. (Book p813)

items.q: The prognosis of calciphylaxis is poor because of:
items.exp: Poor prognosis (↑ risk of secondary infection). (Book p813)

items.q: The treatment pair for calciphylaxis is:
items.exp: Treatment: vit-K + sodium thiosulfate. (Book p813)

items.q: An obese female CKD patient on warfarin develops a painful violaceous plaque on the trunk that nodules and ulcers, with preserved pulses. The diagnosis and treatment pair are:
items.exp: Calciphylaxis: vit-K antagonist precipitant; female obese; violaceous painful plaque → nodule → ulcer; pulse preserved; Rx vit-K + sodium thiosulfate. (Book p813)

items.q: Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis is a scleroderma-like illness caused by:
opts: Gadolinium-based contrast, often with GFR <30 ml/min
items.exp: NSF (scleroderma like illness): cause — gadolinium based contrast often GFR <30 ml/min. (Book p813)

items.q: The GFR below which gadolinium-based contrast is listed as the cause of NSF is:
items.exp: Gadolinium based contrast, often GFR <30 ml/min. (Book p813)

items.q: The photograph set for NSF shows:
opts: Finger contracture; swelling and fibrosis of hands and legs; peau d'orange
Dense periarticular calcification deposits on the film
Violaceous painful plaques on the trunk, pulse preserved
Blue, mottled toes after cardiac catheterization
items.exp: NSF photographs: contracture of fingers; swelling and fibrosis of hands and legs and peau d'orange appearance. (Book p813)

items.q: Atheroembolic renal disease is signposted by:
items.exp: Atheroembolic renal disease: blue toes. (Book p813)

items.q: Match the following entity to its signature finding — 1) Calciphylaxis  2) NSF  3) Atheroembolic renal disease … A) Blue toes  B) Peau d'orange, finger contracture  C) Violaceous painful plaque, pulse preserved
items.exp: As described across the page: calciphylaxis (plaque → nodule → ulcer, pulse preserved); NSF (peau d'orange, contracture of fingers); atheroembolic (blue toes). (Book p813)

items.q: All but one are causes of the fibrotic/calcific skin-vascular syndromes on this page. Which is the odd one out?
items.exp: Page entities: calciphylaxis (vit-K antagonist precipitant), NSF (gadolinium-based contrast), atheroembolic disease. Radiotherapy is not on the page. (Book p813)
